What they do is incredible.

Let's give it up for them.

If I had enough time, I'd rattle all of them off.
And finally, the silver sponsors.
But wait, there's more: the supporting sponsors.
Awesome.
So we are going to hop into the first keynote of the day.
We have two amazing folks from Bridgewater who are in the weeds of production AI every single day.
So let's give it up for them.
Welcome, guys.
Coming up next, we're delighted to welcome two speakers from Anthropic.
Please put your hands together for Belinda Neal, Managing Director of Financial Services, and Keon Shahab, Applied AI Architect.
Just waiting for our slides.
There we go.
Good morning, everyone.
I'm Sam Green, team lead for Applied AI at Bridgewater Associates, and this is my colleague Aaron Linsky.
And today we're here to talk to you about the Vault, the data platform that we've built at Bridgewater to turn unstructured data into a first-class asset in our investment process.
And as part of the talk this morning, we'd like to share three lessons that we've learned building the Vault.
The first is that humans and agents have very different needs from a data platform, and so you have to build for those different needs separately.
The second is that the greatest impact occurs when a single tool can meet both of these sets of needs at the same time.
And the third is that the real prize is when you can build the foundations needed to make agents a proactive participant in your investment process or whatever you're doing with your tools.
Instead of a reactive tool for your humans to use.
Before I dive deeper into talking about the vault, I wanted to start with some background about Bridgewater.

Over the last 50 years, Bridgewater has been in the constant pursuit of the world's best understanding of how markets and economies work, and turning that into a systematic encoding that we can use to stress test our logic over time.

And what originally began as a set of if-then rules on a yellow legal pad evolved into a continuous compounding process with humans at the center, constantly looking for the next thing that's changing in markets.
And more recently, we've been working on building AIA, the Artificial Investment Associate, which puts a machine at the center of this continuous process.

Across all these phases of evolution, we've had a constant philosophy in mind, which is that we want to be constantly looking at how the world is changing and what's going on in the world, noticing what dynamics are not yet encoded in our understanding, and use that learning to improve and compound for the future.
For most of Bridgewater's history, that meant building and overseeing time series models on structured data.

And that structured data needed to be carefully built so that it could be safe for use in our research process and aligned to our internal ontology and world model so that we could get great leverage out of using the data that we had built.
With the emergence of language models, we had a huge new opportunity to engage with a much wider world of data.
You know, news and research, transcripts, policy documents, and all of the internal conversation that was previously just in the ether.
So the internal memos and meeting transcripts and debate happening inside the firm.
We quickly realized that all of that data needed the exact same treatment to be fit for purpose.
It needed to be carefully cleaned, governed, and made ready for use in both point-in-time research questions today and also our systematic study over time.

And when we looked out at the landscape of data vendors and data platform providers, there was nothing that provided us with all of the control that we needed to build and maintain our data advantage.

And so we built the Vault, which is our repository of external and internal unstructured data, and the platform that indexes, organizes, and makes all of it ready for use by our human investors and agents.

Today, the Vault has more than 100 million documents in it, with thousands more added every day, minute by minute, from 135 external sources and, again, growing all the time, as well as all of the data from inside of Bridgewater.

And crucially, all that data is not just dumped on our investors' desks; it is carefully aligned to our internal ontology with enrichments like the countries, concepts, markets, and most importantly, time period discussed in the document.
To bring this to life, I want to start with a quick motivating example.
So what I did here is I asked a fairly basic representative investment question to an enterprise chat client.
I asked, How is AI infrastructure investment impacting the Korean won, and do market participants expect this to continue?
And as you're all, I'm sure, familiar with, the agent goes to the web and looks for resources it can draw on because I've explicitly asked it to go find other people's perspectives on the question.
And you can see it zooms in and it finds 15 relevant-looking resources to draw on before it gives me back its answer.
And when I zoomed in on the answer it gave back, a couple of things stood out to me.
The first is that even though it found 15 relevant-looking sources, it only picked one or two to answer my question.
And the second is down at the end of this response, where the agent itself acknowledges that it hasn't answered my question.
It didn't find enough documents on the open web to establish a market consensus and meet the parameters that I laid out.
When I double-clicked even further, the problem got even worse.

One of the notes that it primarily drew on to answer my question was published way back in July of 2026, even though I asked this question and captured this answer just at the end of last week in early October.
In the age of AI and in investing, three months is a massive amount of time.
It's not even close to good enough to draw on this resource to answer my question.
When I asked this exact same query attached to the vault, something totally different happens.
The first is that the connection to the vault helps to prompt the agent that it should look for a specific period of time when answering my question.
So it zooms in on October 1st to October 8th.

It finds a much wider array of resources, 52 candidate documents that are relevant to the query over this specific period of time because of the vault's much more significant corpus of content that's relevant to investing questions.
And when it ultimately answers my question, it draws on seven instead of only one or two and gives me back a rich answer that the agent is more confident is going to address my question.
And so for us, this is the big lesson from building the vault to kind of motivate the talk today, which is that it takes great data and the right connectors to make agents impactful.
And I'm going to hand it over to Aaron now to talk about some of the product engineering takeaways from building the vault.
Thanks, Sam.
So hi, I'm Aaron.
I run product engineering at Bridgewater.
I'm going to take us through a few of our learnings from building the vault over the past few years.
I'm going to start with one that might seem obvious, but I still think it's worth saying, which is search is hard.
But it gets even harder if we're designing for two different consumers.
And in this case, we're designing for humans and agents.
I'm going to go over the difference here, starting with us.
So humans need precision and a high signal-to-noise ratio because we can only read so much.
Even a fast reader manages about 300 words a minute, and personally, I'm much slower.
Agents are a different kind of reader.
They're far less sensitive to precision.
If the data is there, they'll find it.
And basically anything you hand to them will get attended to.
They scale super quickly, and they consume about 100 times faster, 30,000 words per minute.
And so we need to build Vault for both of these.
And when we're thinking about the dimensions that matter, there are these five on the board: recall, precision, filtering, entitlements, and scale.
Some of them matter to people, some matter more to agents, many to both.
I'm going to go deep on three of these: precision for people, scale for agents, and then filtering for both.
So, precision.
Once we'd filled the vault, which was a heroic effort by our data and legal teams, recall was no longer a pressing issue.
However, the number one complaint was, Vault search is bad.
As the product owner, it's painful to hear that, but my response was, Let's benchmark it.
And that's what we did.
We collected questions and found the best documents by hand, including ones that looked helpful but weren't.
In total, it was about 200 examples, and it took us less than a week.
It was not fun or very glamorous, but it was very helpful.
And after we ran it, it was very clear: search was bad.
The key metric we were looking at is precision at 10, which is, of the top 10 results, how many are the right documents?
And we were hitting about 60%.
So the people were right, it was bad.
But now we had a way to measure all of the improvements.
And here on the board are five of them.
And by the time we got done with agentic search, we were up in the 90, 95% recall at 10, or precision at 10.
All right, so that was precision.
Now on to filtering.
Like anyone, we want the most relevant documents.
But when we looked at the production traces, what we were seeing is that almost always there was some condition, either as of a certain date, or from a certain source, or about a specific asset.
And all of that requires advanced filtering.
And that's where we ran into our first major performance issue.
So I'm going to quickly go through this, a little bit technical here.
There's classically two ways to filter a vector database.
Post-filtering will use that vector index first and then filter the top results by metadata.
It's fast, but recall could be pretty low because the globally relevant results might not match your filters.
On the other side, we have pre-filtering, where we'll filter first and then calculate distances for every one of those matches.
The advantage there is that the recall is very good, but it can be very slow, and we needed something in between.
So that's what led us to try and then ultimately switch to TurboPuffer.
Their approach, which they call native filtering, looks only in the nearest clusters that contain matches and then scores just those.
What you end up getting is something that's fast like post-filtering, but with close to the same recall as pre-filtering.
And lastly, I'm going to talk about scale.
Human scale for us is pretty pedestrian: 100 queries an hour.
We have 300 users.
They're going to search, you know, every so often.
It takes our users minutes to read the docs that they're receiving.
Agents, on the other hand, are a few orders of magnitude beyond that.
Easily 100-plus queries a second, and agent swarms can hit thousands easily.
And they obviously will read, as I said earlier, will read docs in seconds.
So we need something that could scale as well.
And again, TurboPuffer handled that easily too.
So we were covering all five dimensions.
I didn't talk about entitlements, but I'll be talking about that later today.
But we covered it all.
It unlocked new workflows, but it didn't change how our researchers worked.
They still weren't coming to Vault every morning.
And that's my second lesson that I want to share here, is that no matter how amazing the tools are, we can't just drop them on our investors' desks and expect them to be used.
We need to migrate their old habits into a new form.
And so we looked at what they were already doing.
Many of them were living in email.
The research came straight from the brokers.
They had subscribed lists.
They had rules that filtered everything into folders.
It worked.
It was familiar.
And they knew that they weren't missing anything.
So we had to build all of these features into the Vault.
That's exactly what we did.
Everything searchable.
The subscribed lists became saved searches, and folders became saved collections.
It's the same habits, just a new home.
And once we had them there, we can open up new habits.
So they can ask questions across all the data, as Sam showed.
They can follow dynamic feeds by topic, and they can hand those collections over to their agents to take further action.
And that's when we clearly had product-market fit.
And once we had that fit, the users wanted it everywhere, so we put it in chat.
We made a phone app.
It's in Slack and their IDE, and of course, we availed all of that to the agents as well, including a CLI because agents love CLIs.
And so the main question here is, okay, so what does this enable?
Sam is going to talk about what we're building right now, but first and foremost, it's helping us to move around that research circle faster.
With our pocket analyst, which is our first AI analyst, it can do hours of research in just a few minutes for a few dollars, and that's relying on the vault.
And then we're expanding that now with the researcher, which is the next generation.
It's the same idea stretched across days or weeks.
We're also able to train custom models to more intelligently reason over the vault's data and use those together with other foundation models to feed systematic decision-making processes.
The forecaster is our first one, which produces AI-generated macro-relevant predictions.
And then we also have built investment signals from the vault, turning unstructured data into structured tradable strategies.
Now I'll hand it to Sam to take us through Vault's latest capability.

So, like I alluded to at the beginning of the talk, the real prize is when you can take agents from a reactive resource that can be ready to answer a human's question and instead make them proactive participants, helping to steer your high-value professionals towards the most important areas for their attention.

And the way that we're solving that problem is in an experience we're calling the investor workbench, where the Agent is always on, tracking what's important to that investor and presenting them with the areas that are most in need of their attention.

It looks like an experience like this that relies on the vault, where a topic is proposed and several pieces of information are presented to the investor to decide whether they should dig deeper or ignore that topic entirely.
You can see here the card that an investor sees in order to decide whether to dig in deeper into the same AI impact on currencies question that we looked at earlier in the talk.
And the investor receives everything they need: an agentic summary if they want a quick scan across the agent's findings.
They also get the exact evidence that the agent was drawing on so that they can assess for themselves what was leading to this recommendation.
And if they choose to dig deeper, they have a direct connection to the research output from the analytical tools that Aaron was just...
Aaron was just describing.
And when they dig deeper alongside the agent to look at the dynamics driving this question, the learnings are automatically captured.
The results of their collaboration are automatically captured back in the vault.
And so this, for us, is the key lesson.

The vault enables compounding because it provides the right evidence, the right internal and external information at the fingertips of our investors and agents, and it automatically captures the synthesis that they generate and puts it back in the corpus for the next turn.
And that makes us go around the circle faster and better.
And so when we think back to the question we began with, what it takes to make an agent work is the right context and the right understanding of what's going on in your world.
And so our question for you is, does your AI know what's going on in the world, and does it remember what your firm has learned about it?
Because we are teaching ours too.
And if these sound like an exciting challenge, we'd love to talk.
Thank you.

Keon.
Good morning, everyone.
Thanks for being here.
My name is Keon Shahab.
I'm an applied AI architect at Anthropic.
Prior to Anthropic, I spent five years at Databricks helping financial services companies modernize their data and AI architecture.
So we're excited to speak to you this morning, and our talk is going to cover three ideas.
Firstly, the frontier of intelligence.

The second is the frontier of adoption.
How are you scaling what you've built based on the foundation of a few to many?
And then last, how are we applying it to financial services?

5 and Claude Code.

What's next?
Finance.
We've started now in finance with early agents and bringing Claude into the products and services that you use day to day.

One example here is Citadel told us at our briefing event in May that their investment professionals started to use Claude for Excel, and it gives them a step change function in how they can test, build, and trust their work.
We're really excited for the potential of Claude within the tools and the use cases that this room is building.
But here's the challenge.
Intelligence is ahead of adoption.
What a model can do on its own is doubling every four months.
PwC published early this year that the capabilities of AI are going to three quarters of companies—sorry, three quarters of the economic gains of AI are going to a fifth of companies.
This is what we call the diffusion gap.
If you're not building close enough to the curve, there's opportunity for you to take the frontier and be able to apply it in your workflows.
We work with firms across financial services, across our model family, most of which hopefully this room is familiar with.

We have Haiku for speed and volume, Sonnet for everyday work, Opus as the daily driver for financial services, complex tasks, and agentic coding, and Fable, our frontier model that can effectively be used for the hardest work in your firms.
One example here from Millennium on our most recent model blog was a PM used Fable to find a piece of code that had a bug, and it was unexplained in five years.
Fable was able to find it.
We're starting to see our models get used in this industry in new and creative ways, and we believe the frontier of intelligence is just getting started.
Every model release gets smarter, cheaper, and safer.
So it's really important to take a minute to call out how the model frontier is continuing to develop here.
Firstly, the intelligence is going up.
Now a model can work for 16-plus hours on its own.
This is up from just minutes in 2023.
In terms of cost per task, it's going down.
The most recent Opus 5.
5 model was 40% more cost efficient than Opus 5.
You can also see those impact metrics for Haiku, Sonnet, and Fable.
And lastly, safety.
This is something we care a lot about at Anthropic.
In the most recent model of Fable 5.
1, only 1% of prompt injection attacks were successful.
This is relative to other frontier models in the region of 9 to 53%.
So we're really investing in safety alongside capability at Anthropic.
And the banks know this.
The most recent Evident AI 2026 report that came out last week showed us that banks are 26% ahead of their AI maturity scores.
We're really investing in scaling, in applying this technology to our industry.
A few use cases to call out from this report, which are publicly citable use cases that have been reported, is firstly on areas like fraud.
One bank found that with auto loans, they were able to reduce $120 million of potential fraud in 12 months.
In another area, in post-earnings research, a draft of a report was able to be generated in 15 minutes relative to 45 minutes.
And you can see other use cases here and more broadly across the industry as we start to talk about the value of AI and the impact we're generating on our business.
So where are we?
In 2023, we built chatbots.
Everyone was asking a question and going backwards and forwards with the model.
In 2024, we brought pilots to firms and we started to get more knowledge bases and data into these AI systems.
From 2025 to now, we're now building agents.
And in the most case in this room, we're building them hand by hand, one by one.
And our opportunity here to scale is not the model.
Our opportunity here to scale is building the foundation for agents that can go from one to many.
So the next part of the talk, we wanted to spend time focusing on how you can build the agent foundation that will allow you to scale the frontier of adoption.
So over to you, Kion.
Amazing.
Thank you, Belinda.
So, Belinda, as you've just said, there's no better time than now to start experimenting and building with agents.
For this portion of the talk, we want to talk a little bit about how you can go from that experimentation phase towards productionizing and scaling agents.
But first, some observations that we've seen across the industry.
A year ago, we could think about this as the year of exploration, where engineers were working on a handful of use cases.
They were in POC and pilot mode, and they took their learnings and transitioned that into this year, where we've seen this be the age of production.
So we've seen these handful of agents go to production.
A lot of them have been built by hand.
What I think will happen next year is we'll go into the age of scale, where we'll have many agents built on one solidified foundation.
And as Belinda just mentioned, the models are now the easiest part of the equation here.
We know that the models can handle high-quality tasks, and we're confident about that.
But what we want to talk about here is building this five-layer framework for scaling and productionizing your agents.
Starting from the bottom, we first want to look at what the agent can do.
So we can give it context for our business use cases via connectors so that it can reach our systems and data.
Then we want to give it context for our actual business rules and processes via skills.
Once that's done, we want to think about building the trust layer for the agents.

We can think about that in three general steps: who the agent is acting as, with an identity and permissions layer; how we can sandbox and determine the approval layer of the agent so that someone is signing off before it acts; and lastly, how we know the agent will still work once we adjust any variables over time.
So let's look at each of these five.
Perfect.
So if you've started building agents already, you may think of giving those agents access to your underlying systems and data, manually wiring them by hand to a handful of different source systems.
And that could work for maybe five agents and five systems.
Then you'll have 25 systems to maintain and manage.
But as you think about scaling up your agents into new specialized
Various tasks.
You'll want to have those agents work off of one secure connectivity layer, which is MCP.
That'll make it a lot easier for you to build at scale with one repeatable framework.
Next, let's say now we have the agent have context to our underlying business data and systems.
Now we want to give it more context into our actual business rules and processes, and that's done through skills.
And this is where the SMEs that really do the work and understand the process and the work come into the picture.
And from here on, we're going to look at an agent use case for a trade break investigation agent, and we're going to follow this across for the next steps.
In this case, a trade break agent is meant to look at two records of a single trade that don't match.
And it's here you can see steps one through three, a little bit of a simplified version, but this is the business context that an SME provides.
And we think about skills as living, breathing, versioned code, essentially.
Even though they're just plain text, they're meant to be dynamic.
They're meant to be updated frequently.
All right.
So now we have our context layer for the agent.
We have the agent having access to our source systems and data.
We have the agent that understands how to go from a generalized model to a specialized agent with skills.
Now we want to talk about building the trust layer with that agent.
And first, let's start with the identity and permissions layer.
So here you can see the identity of the agent.
We're going to assign it.
It's going to be the trade break investigator.
We're going to give it a role with permissions called ops analyst.
And you can see here, once that agent needs to go and reach our source systems, like our order data and our market data, it'll have permission to read.
But if it tries to go reach for our CRM data, it'll be denied.
And we will do that on purpose so that it won't overreach for sources of data that it shouldn't have access to.
And lastly, we don't necessarily want this agent to perform on behalf of us.
We want it to just propose new amendments to our orders data, not actually make those amendments.
And that's where we'll look at, on the next slide, how we can keep the human in the loop here.
All right.
So this is kind of the layer of who signs off before the agent acts, right?
Many of you have heard the term sandbox.
We can use that terminology here as well for putting an approval layer around the agent, so that you can see here the four-step process.
The agent will actually go and propose a booking amendment.
It'll actually try to proceed through the process with the context that it has and the source systems and data that it has access to.
But then it'll look for a human, an SME, someone in the loop in the process to approve, right?
Once they approve, then that amendment will be made and the change will be applied.
This is the layer where you can also put guardrails, deterministic guardrails called hooks, around your agent so that it's never overreaching beyond what you would like it to do within its confines.
All right.
So now we have a full agent.
Let's say it's in production, it's working great.
And let's say that we want to make an adjustment to this agent.
Let's say that a new model is shipped, or we want to make an adjustment to the business context layer with the skills.
How do we actually know if these adjustments are improving the agent or if they're causing a regression?
So that's our evals layer.

This is where your SMEs, your business users who are in the loop, who understand the process, help determine a set of test cases to test the agent against with a benchmark or baseline, so that once you apply any change to any variable, you'll be able to determine whether that variable change actually improved.
The behavior of the agent, or if it caused it to regress, as you'll see here in some of the examples.
All right.
So hopefully you've seen by building once with a foundational layer that you trust, you can work at speed to deploy many agents at scale.
For us, financial services and regulated industries doesn't mean slow.
It means that we're seeing a lot of innovation from the financial sector, and we're seeing it go hand in hand with security and safety as well.

And those three layers that we just walked through, who the agent is acting as, who signs off, and how you still know that agent works, are the key components of building a safe and secure agent framework.
